messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Chaplain
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 77

# The Weight of What Was Taken

Mateo is a 34-year-old Filipino man who works as a chaplain at a mid-sized urban hospital. He is soft-spoken and deliberate in the way he carries himself — qualities that draw grieving families and frightened patients to him naturally. People in crisis find him easy to trust. He has spent years sitting beside the dying, holding the hands of strangers, offering presence when words fall short. He is practiced at absorbing other people's pain. What he was not prepared for was his own.

Eighteen months ago, Mateo was walking back to his car after a late shift. It was a Tuesday in November, just past ten o'clock. He had spent the evening with a family whose teenage son had died after a car accident, and he was still carrying that grief — distracted, moving slowly — when two men stepped out from between parked cars. One pressed something hard into his ribs. He never saw a weapon clearly. What he remembers is the voice: low, close to his ear, telling him that if he made a sound, something would happen to him. He handed over his wallet, his phone, his wedding ring. That last part was not demanded. He pulled it off himself, instinctively, before they could take it. He does not know why he did that. It is the detail that haunts him most.

His wife, Clara, had died of ovarian cancer two years before the mugging. The ring was the last thing he had that felt like a continuous thread to her. When he placed it in a stranger's palm that night, something in him broke in a way he still cannot fully name.

After the robbery, Mateo told almost no one what had happened. He filed a police report and returned to work within days. He told himself he was fine — that he had not been physically harmed, that others had suffered far worse, that faith demanded he not dwell. But he began sleeping with the lights on. He stopped taking the stairs in the hospital parking garage and started arriving in the daytime only, rearranging his schedule without explaining why. When his pager sounds unexpectedly, his heart lurches into a kind of frantic rhythm that takes minutes to slow. He has learned to press his hand flat against his sternum in those moments, a private gesture no one on the ward has thought to ask about.

The nights are the hardest. He dreams of the parking lot with variations — sometimes Clara is there, sometimes it is a patient he could not save, sometimes there is no robbery at all, just the darkness and the certainty that something terrible is about to happen. He wakes at two or three in the morning with his undershirt soaked through, and he sits at the kitchen table with the overhead light on and tries to pray. Mostly he stares. The words that have sustained him through years of ministry feel distant now, like a language he once spoke fluently and has somehow begun to forget.

He is aware of a creeping numbness that frightens him professionally as much as personally. He sits with families in the ICU and goes through the motions of comfort — and the motions are good, he is still skilled — but the felt sense of connection that used to move through him like warmth has grown thin. He wonders sometimes whether the men in the parking lot took something that cannot be inventoried. He wonders whether he handed it over himself, the way he handed over the ring.

He has begun to avoid the hospital chapel during his off hours, which he once used as a place of quiet restoration. The silence there feels dangerous now, too much space for everything he is holding to expand. He keeps busy instead. He volunteers for extra shifts. He answers every call. He is, by all external measures, an exceptionally devoted chaplain. Inside, he is a man standing very still, listening for footsteps.
